newsitem.title: UK: N.Sea crude under pressure, Urals held up by tender.
newsitem.headline: N.Sea crude under pressure, Urals held up by tender.

text.p: North Sea crude differentials were under some pressure to ease downwards in a quiet market on Tuesday, while cash crude markets idled at steady levels, traders said.

Although Brent crude was still firm after a buyer paid seven cents over August on Monday and a British major continued to offer cargoes at 15 cents over the same month, other grades were threatening to drift south.
An Ekofisk cargo loading July 27-29 was traded at fifteen cents over dated Brent, a cent weaker than a deal last Thursday, and eight cents off from last Monday.

"I think all grade premia are under pressure," said one trader. "There is still a fair amount left in the third decade, refinery margins are not great and it won't be long before we see the differentials slip."
Overall physical markets were quiet, although some "window shopping" was reported.

Cash markets were sleepy with spreads steady. Prompt contracts for differences were offered higher by one player making a market play but were bid much lower and stood at 0.00/+0.15 against August. They were at +0.05/+0.08 on Monday while the Brent sale went through.
In the Mediterranean dealers were scratching their heads over the 67 cents below dated Brent paid for a July 11-13 loading Urals on Monday. It was described as "a very solid number."
Traders complained Turkey's tender to buy 300,000 tonnes of crude had badly unsettled the market, boosting numbers above the -80 to -75 cents currently thought reasonable.

They said the tender by state oil company Tupras, announced on Monday and due to close at the end of the week, may fail as it was unlikely there was enough Urals available to supply the amount wanted in the July 15-25 window specified.

"There are so few people able to offer Urals that the Turks may have to go for different grades or postpone their tender when they see the prices they'll be quoted," said one seller. "That's put a lot of uncertainty into the market."
Without the Turkish tender, and despite the continued absence of Iraqi barrels, Urals prices would have begun to drift down, traders said.
